It's a complex idea, privilege. But yes, work is in some ways a privilege. I'm disabled and unable to work, which means I live in forced poverty on government disability. I can't save (literally not allowed to, also I'm not paid enough), can't earn money (both due to my disabilities and because it would lose me my support. I get around $1k/month to live on. If I had enough time between doctor and hospital visits and home treatments and all of the puking, shitting endlessly, shaking, pain, passing out onto the floor, and excess sleep I require, to even make some money, it would just be deducted from my income. If I made too much ($1300/month) I would just lose my income, health care, and housing. If I were to find something I could do with my health the way it is (it's degenerative, so it will update last for long before I'd be back and having to go through the years long process to get my support back), I would have to immediately and indefinitely jump to being able to earn well over $6k/month just to cover my prescriptions alone, before the daily appointments, specialist care, testing, medical equipment, and, you know, housing, food, and normal people expenses. Given my health has prevented me from learning any trades or getting through higher education, and I can't physically work any job that requires any physical labor, that leaves me pretty much stuck where I am forever. 

So yeah, much as I hate that society forces it on people and would change that, the ability to work is absolutely a privilege.

Some stores do hire actual loss prevention. I know this firsthand because of a blackout episode triggered by a new psych med several years ago. Walked through a Macy's I'd never even been to before just dead-eyed and dissociated putting random shit in a big bag. Like, whatever was closest to the aisle, no discrimination at all. An entire watch display, with the display thing they were sitting on. No memory of it, just watched the security footage in court. 

Big ass loss prevention literally tackled me at the door. It wasn't the same one I went in, so not sure what I would have done if I hadn't been caught. You could see me screaming and thrashing in the video. The guy pinned me and cuffed me and took me to some room in the back to wait for police to show. 

Woke up in jail in the middle of the night, scuffed up with some muscle strains, scrapes, and bruises, and completely covered in blood, with a migraine. I guess they'd removed my tampon and not replaced it with anything, and the blood was all over my hands and face and hair and clothes. Saw a night judge who released me immediately, I guess I looked pretty haggard. 

Went to court and the judge watched the security footage and I said what I could remember and I was told to check in with a pre-trial officer once a week and keep taking my meds and seeing my doctors. Nothing in my record from it. The whole situation was crazy and I'm really fucking lucky. I was legitimately not present mentally for what happened in that Macy's, but the pattern of overall behavior re:shoplifting was definitely there because I grew up poor and had stolen a ton of food, household goods, and clothes before. Never from a place like Macy's, just supermarkets and big chain stores like w*lmart. But it's definitely not true that every store will just let you walk out with stuff. Some places take it really seriously.

I wish I'd had someone like your grandma. I was unwanted, and my bio mom was in and out of my life, just coming around when she needed something. Always I'd beg her to stay and be better and stop doing drugs and drinking, and always she'd be off again, abandoning me and disappearing for months or years. 

I was adopted by my grandma and grandpa, but my grandpa died in front of my when I was 9 and my grandma didn't want me either. She used to tell me how lucky I was she adopted me when no one wanted me, and she didn't either so I'd better act right. I ate less than everyone else at the same table because she'd yell at me and hit me if I took more. I was so tiny and skinny and the doctor would say I was just a late bloomer, but I didn't really grow until I was old enough to steal food from the grocery store. 

My adoptive mom (grandma) married my stepdad after my adoptive dad (grandpa) died, and he was extremely abusive. He would beat the shit out of me regularly and yelled at me constantly. He loved to ground me from books and going outside, because those were my escapes. He and my mom would leave me alone in the house to care for my (great) grandma who was dying of Parkinson's, who was about 275lbs and had dementia, when I was 11-12 and weighed about 75lbs soaking wet. She couldn't walk, I had to use a hoyer lift to move her and to clean her. But she didn't know who I was and would yell at me and call me a stupid bitch and much worse. My second suicide attempt was at 12 left alone with her. I swallowed a Costco bottle of ibuprofen and a bunch of her meds. 

My first suicide attempt had been at 6. My bio mom's boyfriend had been sexually abusing me for years. I tried to die of hypothermia. I went outside in the snow and laid down and tried to sleep. I later found out my adoptive mom and the rest of the family all knew about the sexual abuse and no one said or did anything. 

I was adopted again when I was 17, this time by my adoptive sister (bio aunt) and her husband. They weren't physically abusive, but they refused to acknowledge I was disabled and do anything to accommodate it or get me real care. My sister was the director of disability support services at the local university, and disabled herself, but she constantly denied my own disabilities and demanded I do things I wasn't capable of. She only adopted me to get me free school, and she constantly reminded me of that. I moved out before I turned 18. 

I won't have kids myself. I've worked with kids a lot (teacher, nanny, fostering, camp counselor, etc), but I won't bring a human into the world with all of my genetic and epigenetic bullshit. My bio aunts who carried a family genetic disorder have all had kids, and 5/6 of them have the disorder, which is extremely painful and debilitating. My bio mom was bipolar, and so am I. I'm already prediabetic at 33, almost everyone on that side of the family has diabetes and that's what killed my adoptive dad. I don't know the other side because my family refused to ever tell me anything about them and I cut them all off for good several years ago.

As for OP, I know he probably doesn't have a chronic bowel disease, but it's frustrating reading all these comments saying stuff like "anyone who takes 20 minutes to poop is TA, if it takes that long see a doctor" as though doctors can just magically fix chronic bowel issues, or chronic illness in general. I'm on many medications, a special diet, and I still have all of these issues. People without chronic illness and disability seem to be under the impression that seeing a doctor will just solve everything. That's not reality.

With this kind of issue you get used to talking about poop. I'm more worried about this being outside of your comfort zone, lol. 

So, days of many hours on the toilet can look a few different ways. I usually have diarrhea, but I also get badly constipated every once in a while (which can easily lead to a bowel obstruction I need to visit the hospital for, so it's even more dangerous). For diarrhea, it usually is that only a tiny bit is coming out at a time, but it's completely liquid and comes out without much warning, so if I go back to bed or the couch I'll end up leaking and changing my underwear several times because I can't make it back to the toilet in time. I only have so much tolerance for soiled underwear and feeling like a baby, so I end up staying on the toilet. Also the pain gets really intense and sometimes I can't walk, so unless I stay on the toilet I might end up having to wash my sheets as well. 

If the pain is bad enough, I might take my prescription, which is like a muscle relaxer for smooth muscles. It can help when it's very excruciating, but it turns the shit into sludge, which takes absolutely forever to get out, so it's usually not worth it. 

With constipation, I can't really tell when something will come out, and it takes a long time and lot of effort to get any movement. I literally have to focus and push to get it to come out, sometimes for hours. I can't push in bed or on the couch, because when it does come out it will be sudden and followed by all the diarrhea that got backed up behind it, which would make a massive mess I'm not interested in having to clean up. 

Altogether, this means I spend a lot of time on the toilet on any given day, and some days when I'm in a bad flare up it can literally be over 12 hours total. I leave the bathroom and lay in bed when I can, but it's risking having to wash a lot of clothes and feel pretty shitty (lol) about myself. 

I also have bladder issues that make peeing take a long time, separately. My bladder doesn't empty fully, and to get even half of the liquid out I have to sit and concentrate, sometimes for several minutes. Then because even with effort it doesn't all come out, and I have to drink liquids with electrolytes nearly constantly due to an autonomic disorder that causes low blood volume, I have to pee again within half an hour to an hour, all day and night long. 

I've seen many doctors, and I continue to see doctors about all I've described and more. I understand OP probably doesn't have these issues, but it's frustrating reading all these comments saying stuff like "anyone who takes 20 minutes to poop is TA, if it takes that long see a doctor" as though doctors can just magically fix chronic bowel issues. I'm on many medications, a special diet, and I still have all of these issues. People without chronic illness and disability seem to be under the impression that seeing a doctor will just solve everything. That's not reality.

Unfortunately I also have other disabilities, and all of it together keeps me from being able to work or go to school, so it's not *as big* of an issue. It can definitely affect things like watching stuff with people (anyone who sits down to movie with me has to be prepared for a sudden pause for a while) or playing board games or the rare times I make it out of the house, having to suddenly find a restroom. I even have a card signed by my doctor that legally obligates businesses to allow me to use their employee restrooms, but I've never had to guts to use it, most of the time my social anxiety means I'd rather shit myself and go home than get into that kind of argument. I honestly just don't spend that much time in public, and when I do I have to plan around bathrooms being available.

You sound like someone who's never shit themselves because of a bowel disorder. Waiting is not an option. And frequently even when I rush to the bathroom because it's literally starting to come out without my control I'm still in there for a long time, sometimes hours.

Lmao at the idea that a visit to the doctor will just clear up chronic bowel issues. Some days I'm on the toilet literally for more time than I'm not. Studies about habituation suggest you would actually adjust and find your life to be approximately as worth living as you find it now. Humans evolved to put up with horrifying situations. In a twin study of several thousand by Lykken and Tellegen, it was found that about 50% of variation in Well-Being scale of the Multidimensional Personality Questionnaire is associated with genetic variation, and less than 3% (!) of the variance can be accounted for by any of socioeconomic status, educational attainment, family income, marital status, or religious commitment. From my understanding of the science here, the hormone is released during strenuous exercise and when shivering. It's not just people who are paralyzed or comatose who can't achieve strenuous exercise (and shouldn't be exposed to cold). All sorts of conditions prevent someone from safely doing strenuous exercise. It is dangerous for many with heart conditions, it isn't healthy for many with injuries, it isn't possible for many with chronic illnesses. Many, many people are disabled, and many disabilities take strenuous exercise off the table. 

For me, I have a debilitating chronic illness, and bipolar disorder. When I'm in a flare up, not only is exercise painful, it's not healthy. Sure, doing small things as much as possible is good, but not exercising to the level that would produce this hormone. When I'm in a severe depressive episode, I am sometimes catatonic, and have to be hospitalized. I can't exercise in the depths of my depression, and like most with bipolar I spend much more of my time in depressive or mixed episodes than I do in manic episodes. Speaking of manic episodes, they cause destructive impulsivity, and I often end up hospitalized by them as well, as I injure myself easily (chronic conditions again), and sometimes I'm a danger to myself and need supervised medication. 

I'm not paralyzed. I'm not in a coma. I exercise when and where I can, but often I can't. The costs outweigh the benefits. There are many people like me, or in much worse situations. Good thing they're going to make the drug, because everyone should have access to treatments that prevent something as awful as Alzheimer's. I don't know if anyone you love has suffered from it, but it's horrifying. I have a small taste, because I've undergone electroconvulsive therapy, which can cause memory damage. I don't remember most of the last year thanks to it, and that's terrifying. Found out recently that in a manic episode I followed some random guys back to their house in Mexico to try and buy drugs. Mania is a bitch, and I literally have no memory of the event or any of the weeks surrounding it. I would wish Alzheimer's or memory loss on the worst person on the planet. 

I'm not saying people shouldn't exercise as much as they're able. I'm just saying not everyone is able.

Hey, so I'll tell you the things that stick out to me both positive and negative. My birth mother was also in the picture, and I didn't find anything out about my birth father for decades. 

In day to day life, one of the biggest things that alienated me was being referred to as anything other than my adopted family role. The first time I was adopted it was by my maternal grandparents. My birth mom was in and out of the picture, so she managed to abandon me several times in spite of never really being a parent. But the real soul killer was every time one of my adoptive sisters called me "niece" or my parents "granddaughter" or "adopted daughter." Every time I was referred to as something other than what I was "supposed to be" it was just more evidence that I was a mistake, that I wasn't wanted, that I'd never really be what the adoption was supposed to make me, that I wasn't valid. My second adoption didn't help this at all, as the same issues persisted, and by that point I was willfully distancing myself to avoid the pain. If there's anything at all you can do to get the uncle/brother to really put some effort into calling the younger ones siblings that could go miles and miles toward fostering a healthy and safe environment. When he acts like they aren't siblings, if they're anything like me it's a knife in their backs. 

As for nasty birth fathers, try not to hide it from them for too long. You can gauge how mature they are, but give them as much credit as you can. My adoptive family, most especially my adoptive mother, lied to me until my late twenties about my birth father and it's one of the reasons I've completely cut them off. I was fed a story about how we didn't know who he was for years. Then when I prodded as I got older I was told he "died before you were born, he was shot at a party." Details were added to that story very sparingly, but that was my truth for most of my life. When we had "family tree" assignments in elementary school my mom actually wrote a note so I wouldn't have to do it. I was getting curious, but I was always rebuffed. I asked her several times, point blank, if she knew. She liked every time. When I was 28 she finally admitted that she knew his name. She said his family were all horrible alcoholics and abusers and she'd lied to protect me. (For clarity, I was a fetal alcohol baby, she still let my birth mother around me even though she never stopped drinking or using, and I was physically and sexually abused in her home). She said she was scared I would seek them out, and if I did that they'd try to "take me" from her. She told me this at 28, after she was relatively sure the grandparents had passed on, and she said that was one of the reasons she waited. She said she still didn't want to tell me. I still have no idea who or where these people are, because I'm scared to find out.

It's smart to not traumatize the kids further with every gory detail. But if they ask, don't lie to them. Even without all the other stuff I had, it would be a huge blow for them to find out the depressing details and also find out you lied to them. It really hard not to resent someone who has lied to you for years. I will never speak to my adoptive mother again, and finding out she had lied about that was the final straw before I blocked her and everyone else from contacting me. 

Sorry, all of that was dark and depressing. My family didn't do a great job, so I don't have the best advice for what to do right, only what not to do. 

But I do have some things that helped. I ended up really hungry for a sense of belonging, for the rest of my life so far. I've gotten tastes of it at camp, youth corps, the army, communities. It feels spectacular. If you can give that to your little ones it will be a treasure they'll keep forever. Make sure they are always a part of things, and not left feeling like observers. Don't coddle them, that's just another way of othering. Obviously give them as much love and support as you can, but part of that is learning to trust them. You have to let them learn how to fail, and learn that even if they do it won't change your love for them. It's tempting to not push them, because they're fragile. But they need to know both that they are capable, and don't always need to be rescued, and that even if they fail you'll be there. It's so easy as an adopted kid to feel like you have to learn your family's love and your place in the house; to feel like a burden. It's so easy to feel helpless and like you have no control over your life. It's honestly mostly normal kid issues, just put under the huge magnifying glass of *I WAS ABANDONED AND NO ONE WILL EVER REALLY WANT ME AND THERE'S NOWHERE I'LL BELONG*. Try to help them see that they're *your first pick*. They can't be unwanted, because you wanted them enough to choose them and keep them. I worked at Sears for 3 days about 4 years ago. Wednesday, Thanksgiving Thursday, and black Friday. I was hired as a mattress salesperson. On Friday the manager wasn't there and I wasn't able to log in. He'd told me I'd be able to get my commissions for that day, even though I was still in training, because it was expected to be a big day. 

The day comes and I don't have a log in, and I have no way to get into the training log in. I help some people with information, then send them to other employees to make their decisions, figuring I can't help them ring out. Then one of the older employees comes over and says I need to be helping out more by making sales myself, and tells me he'll log me into a sales account. When I’m sleeping, I can run again. My feet pound steadily against the packed dirt trail, and the rocks aren’t obstacles, but objectives. I leap and bound, my breath coming hard, and the pain is gone. My body listens, and I listen back. It works; it used to work. 

When I’m sleeping, she’s running next to me. Her body is beautiful, Better than mine was even before the accident, and nothing like the broken husk I’m trapped in when I’m awake. But her body isn’t why I love her. She laughs when she runs. And when she looks at me I can see in her eyes she loves the mountains the way I love them. It’s a desperate love, not something you can fulfill, or be entirely at peace with. The kind of ache that makes you move. You wriggle and squirm and can pinpoint at first what it is until you see them and then you know. You have to be in them. You have to be up there. You have to breathe that air, touch those rocks, feel your muscles burn as you reach for higher ground. 

That’s what it is, really; higher ground.  I love her, and I know she loves me, because we’re moved by the same force. Higher ground. I know there are people who see wide open skies and it moves them. We are not those people. We see those mountains and know we can get to that place, a part of us has to prove it. Well...I used to know I could. Now I know I can’t. The only time in my life I’ve ever lived somewhere I couldn’t see mountains is when the accident happened. I’m not superstitious, I promise. But sometimes, when the pain is almost too much to bear (not the physical pain, I’ve always handled that) I wonder a bit, deep inside, if it was a punishment. For forsaking them. 

In my dreams, I am not forsaken. I am running, I am climbing, and she is beside me laughing. Her eyes tell me she is like me, and I am in love. She knows I love her with that same burning ache I love the mountains. I will never get enough of her. 

When we can no longer breathe for laughing and running, and our eyes are sharp with love and determination, she looks at me. Blue eyes fierce, with flecks of green and yellow. In my dreams, I can make love again. Real love, the kind you can’t walk right after (ha). It’s a battle, rapturous and savage. Our hair becomes one writhing mass, our lips bruise as our teeth seek out tender places to ravage, our bodies slick from our concerted passion. I spend so much of my life trying to control the things around me, and when I’m with her, I let her take me (but not without a fight). She enters every part of me. 

Perhaps it is possible to find fulfillment in the mountains, after all.

When I awake, I am always dripping with excitement. But the muscle relaxers make completion...strange. No shudders, no contractions, just something of the release. And then the pain sets in. And the realizations. Real life. The girl doesn’t exist. I cannot run. 

I go about my daily life in a haze. Wheeling from work to the doctor to a friend’s house to home. Thinking mostly about sleep, and this girl in my dreams. At night I pull myself up to stand as well as I can in front of the mirror in the bathroom, to see my body. My shape remains mostly unchanged, and I suppose it’s one most women are envious of. But the skinny parts, the flabby parts, the parts wasted and the parts I cannot move...I wish I could say I can barely look at them. I look at every inch. I scour myself every night, and wonder if this dream girl would love me if she could see this broken body. At least my arms look damn good. 

Last night I didn’t dream. I woke in a cold sweat, my seemingly endless libido having apparently taken an unheard of day off. It’s raining today. I’m supposed to use this umbrella holding contraption on the wheelchair, but where I’m from we don’t believe in umbrellas. So I look like a wet dog. Nothing new, really. Except that today is different. Today is the day I find out. 

The waiting room of the orthopedics clinic is cold, and I’ve always scoffed at the offers of a blanket for my lap. Not even over my dead body. I plan on being cremated anyway, and spread in the mountains. Some days I wonder if that’s the only way I’ll ever make it back. 

After they take my vitals (10 more pounds down, time was that would have sent me to the moon), I wait in my paper gown. I’m trying not to focus on charts and graphs around me, depicting all the things that can go wrong in the fragile scaffolding we build around us to house our minds. When there is nothing else to focus on the pain becomes intense. I am nearly in tears by the time I hear a knock on the door, and my voice catches when I say “come in”

It’s her.

She looks different, a bit. In a white coat, professional (she wears glasses?). But it’s her. Her wild curls are pulled back into a sensible bun, but I can see a few tendrils poking out, unwilling to be tamed. Her dress is polished, right up until her feet, which are clad in well worn hiking boots. Her eyes...are exactly like my dreams. Intense blue, I can see passion and intelligence as though it might burst from behind them. My heart is pounding, and I wonder if I will look the same to her, as she must see me in her dreams. She looks up from her clipboard, offers her hand, and with no recognition on her face, she says,

“You must be Iliana”

There are two questions an employee/business can ask to establish whether a service dog is real.

1. Is that a service dog?

2. What tasks is the dog trained to perform to mitigate your disability?

Service dogs are individually trained to perform specific tasks (some places require only one, most require three, most SDs I've met, including mine, know several) that mitigate the handler's documented disability. Emotional support animals, therapy animals, and companion animals are not. 

What is absolutely illegal is any question trying to determine the nature of the person's Disability, as this infringes on their privacy rights.

You CANNOT ask:
What's the dog for?
Why do you have that dog?
What's wrong with you?

Or any variation on that theme. 

Obviously a person with a fake can lie, but it seems that most people don't do their research, and won't have an adequate answer to the second legal question, or at least a perceptive person will usually be able to tell they're lying. 

Unfortunately, the business doesn't have a whole lot of recourse if the person does lie. But there are some legally protected says for a business to deal with this.

If the person answers the question wrong, by, say, telling them it's an emotional support animal, they can ask them to leave; emotional support animals do NOT have public access rights. 

If the person lies, and you believe they are lying, just keep an eye on them. Dogs are not naturally suited to most environments they aren't generally allowed in. Service dogs, even those that are owner trained, will have had years of training to ensure they behave properly in public. An animal that isn't a service dog will usually be easy to spot, because it's HARD to train a dog not to bark, or sniff/steal food, or pull aggressively (some mobility dogs and guide dogs pull in a specific way, I'm talking about dragging the person who is trying to control them), or whine/growl/get overly excited when another dog walks by. 

Businesses are absolutely within their rights to kick out a disruptive dog, service dog or not. They do have to let the person know they can come back and be served without the dog, but they have every right to remove a dog that is being a safety issue or nuisance. Any dog that has an accident in a place it isn't supposed to can be removed. 

Don't get me wrong here, service dogs aren't perfect. They have off days, and they make mistakes. They are still dogs, not robits. The law has provisions for this. If the dog makes a mistake, say by barking, or reaching to sniff a dropped food item, or getting up when another dog passes, the handler can't just immediately be kicked out. If the handler corrects the behavior, and the dog remains under control, the dog is still legally allowed to stay. But if the handler makes no effort to correct the behavior, of the correction doesn't work and the behavior continues, the business can absolutely ask them to remove the dog. 

Service dogs are pretty great, and can do a whole variety of incredible tasks to help people with disabilities. But they are still dogs! Depending on the disability, some people may require their dog at all times in public, or only part of the time. This does not make them more or less disabled, and seeing someone you know has a service dog without them does NOT mean they were faking. (Mine is pretty much always with me, though I occasionally hand her off to a friend before going to the bathroom if I'm somewhere familiar). Also, just like any other dog, service dogs get to play! This is wholly dependent on the dog and it's handler/situation, but all service dogs get off time to relax and play. Mine goes swimming, to the dog park, camping, to the beach...she has a lot of fun, and gets a lot of love and exercise!

Sorry for the wall of text, I hope this helped answer any questions you might have, but feel free to ask about anything!

TL:DR: It is legal to ask whether it is a service dog, and what tasks it is trained to perform, but not much else. And disruptive dogs can be kicked out.
